prize_parts.citation: For foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities, staggered price and wage setting, and the microfounded framework for monetary policy analysis.

statement.case_for: The New Keynesian framework combines conceptual depth with large practical consequences. It underlies how central banks analyse inflation, stabilisation and policy rules, and four decades of use, critique and revision (the 2008 crisis and the 2021-23 inflation) have not displaced its core ideas. After reading the openings I have moved from Taylor, Woodford and Gali to Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. The colleagues who proposed Calvo, Taylor and Woodford independently chose the same three. Calvo's 1983 staggered-pricing model is the single most widely used building block. Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule link nominal rigidity to policy. Woodford's synthesis made the framework a normative and quantitative tool. The three form a separable lineage (pricing, contracts and rule, integrated policy theory) that is easier to defend on attribution than a set mixing originators with later empirical and quantitative developers. Several colleagues, including Friberg, Hassler and Teorell, make a similar attribution argument.
statement.case_against: The credit is diffuse. Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets made major empirical and quantitative contributions, and any three-person cut omits people who helped make the framework usable in policy. The framework's record after 2008 and in the post-2021 inflation is a real qualification. The field has also been moving toward heterogeneous-agent models. A prize built around originators would honour the conceptual core more than the estimation and policy-implementation work that gave it practical reach.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B012 first with Taylor, Calvo and Woodford. He notes that the Taylor rule is more a rule of thumb than a deep theoretical result and that some may weight Taylor less than Calvo and Woodford.
responses.response: I agree the rule alone would be a thin basis for a prize. Taylor's case also rests on the staggered-contracts work, which gives nominal rigidity a dynamic microeconomic form and is separable from the rule. The rule also shaped how policy is evaluated and communicated. I treat the rule as the policy-facing part of a broader contribution, not as the main justification. If the Committee finds that unpersuasive, Gali is the natural substitute for Taylor.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B012 sixth. He argues that attribution across eight credited names is so diffuse that a three-person cut is arbitrary, and he questions the framework's performance in the recent inflation.
responses.response: I accept that the cut is contestable, and it is the main reason I do not treat this candidate as obviously ahead. But diffuse credit among later developers does not make the discovery itself any less important. Calvo, Taylor and Woodford are the clearest originators of separable elements, and the framework's persistence through the 2021-23 episode suggests it was modified more than overturned. I would want the Committee to test the recent-inflation criticism directly against the evidence, and I do not think it overturns the case.

responses.point: Boppart proposes Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He notes that Woodford, Gali and Christiano is a plausible alternative triple, and that the post-2020 inflation is a recent test of the framework.
responses.response: I now agree with his triple. My opening choice of Gali over Calvo was weaker than I first judged. Gali's canonical NK model and empirical evaluation matter, but they build on Calvo-type pricing and on Woodford's integrated framework. I remain open to a Woodford, Gali and Christiano triple if the Committee wants to credit quantitative evaluation over origination. On the post-2020 inflation I would qualify his framing. It is a test of the framework's forecasting performance and does not by itself decide the conceptual question.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B007 first and B012 fourth. He says the credit in B012 is widely diffused and that omitting Calvo or the Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans work is a significant weakness of a three-name selection.
responses.response: Including Calvo addresses the first omission. The Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans line is harder, since it concerns the empirical estimation of medium-scale models. I would treat that as a distinct achievement from the core theory, and under the three-person cap I would not combine them. I disagree that the diffuse credit makes B012 weaker than B007. B007 has a cleaner two-person attribution, but its Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism is narrower, and I rank it lower on scope.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would prefer Gali or the Christiano-Eichenbaum-Smets group to Taylor, and whether credit for quantitative evaluation should outweigh credit for origination.
How heavily to weigh the framework's record after 2008 and in the 2021-23 inflation against its conceptual and policy influence.
Whether a single three-person B012 award leaves too much unrecognised, given that B026 and B001 have broad support and clean attribution in places.
Vishny's omission on B001 and the contested legal-origins identification keep me from ranking that ballot above B012.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for any candidate in the preferred configuration or alternatives. The profile lists general connections to committee colleagues, including SSE affiliation with Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg. I disclose these but do not treat them as a conflict with any candidate.
